title: AlphaDestiny Novice Program review (part. 2: FAQ)
summary: NH goes through the FAQ of AlphaDestiny's novice program, correcting his earlier mistake (it's 3 days/week, ABA/BAB). He agrees on most points (no Smith squats, bodyweight chins, deficit deadlifts, isolation for calves/neck) but disagrees on stall handling (also raise volume), failure definition, equipment bans, box squats with high-bar wide stance, floor press, trap work, and no forearm work. Verdict: it works.

claims.claim: Correction: the program is 3 days a week (Mon/Wed/Fri, alternating ABA/BAB), which makes it much better; weekends off are important for novices and alternating workouts is simple.
The program's 2-5 minute rest guideline between sets is good.
Telling novices not to modify a program is acceptable because novices need to be babied a bit.
The program's undulating set/rep scheme shows volume manipulation is simple, even if novices don't realise they're doing it.
How you handle a stall matters. The program says take 10% off the stalled lift and build back; he says you should also increase volume, raising tonnage, which leads to progress again.
He disagrees that plateaus naturally multiply as you approach intermediate; they multiply because the programs people run are poorly written.
If your upper body is intermediate but your lower body isn't, just work the lagging part.
Failing reps is bad, but always getting the rep just short of technical or actual failure, with clean form, is not 'going to failure' and is what you should do.
Novices can recomp easily; unless very fat or very skinny they shouldn't worry much about bulking vs cutting, but should learn basic dieting.
He has no experience cutting, so won't comment on cutting volume.
Box squats and trap bar deadlifts aren't better for recreational lifters, just easier; a recreational lifter serious about bodybuilding should do something else.
Use whatever equipment you like (belts, straps, sleeves) as long as it doesn't modify the lift's strength curve; if it helps recovery or strength, use it. He has never used a belt himself.
Equipment that adds a lot of poundage, like wraps and slingshots, needs thought and novices shouldn't use it.
He never does 1-rep maxes and doesn't use bands or chains; he trains with straight weight.

He disputes the claimed box-squat benefits (better recovery, less knee pain, explosiveness): people rock and good-morning the weight up, the wide stance barely uses quads, and the stressed range may create imbalances leading to knee pain.
A lift that cuts range of motion is subpar for building explosiveness through full ROM.

Box squats carry over to the deadlift because you push from roughly hip-height of the pull, but quad and glute development won't be maximised; full ROM squats are better, and box-only squatters are surprised how little carries to free squats.
Squat high or low bar as you prefer; high-bar wide-stance box squats are about as far from a proper squat as you can get, since you want to train the legs, not the hips.
He loves front squats but not for novices because they are very technical.
Never squat in the Smith machine.
Overhead press and overhead extensions don't replace horizontal pressing; novices need several horizontal presses (push-ups, dips or bench), but floor press isn't needed.
Novices shouldn't worry about upper chest; normal bench works it well.
He prefers full range of motion on the overhead press, down to the collarbone area.

Overhead extensions are worth doing for the triceps long head; standard skull crushers miss it because most people do them without shoulder flexion. But overhead extensions can cause elbow pain, so novices should be careful and use dumbbells if it hurts.
Novices' traps can grow from heavy deadlifts and rows, but past the novice phase that is absolutely not enough; trap work is needed.
Everyone should do chin-ups with bodyweight before adding weight.
Trap bar and conventional deadlifts aren't the same; try both. He doesn't like the behind-the-back (hack) deadlift at all.
If you sumo deadlift, pair it with close-stance high-bar squats without a box rather than wide-stance box squats.
Novices shouldn't do Jefferson deadlifts or snatch-grip deadlifts; snatch-grip is too technical for novices (recovery cost depends on leverages, load and reps).
He loves deficit deadlifts for novices because they teach pushing with the legs.
Block pulls suit those with lower back issues and can be a deload that lets lifters pull more than once or twice a week, but novices don't need them.
Only replace deadlifts with rack pulls if you have to; between good mornings and stiff-leg deadlifts pick whichever you can do safely.
Adding a few sets of reverse hypers or hyperextensions at the end of a program doesn't hurt.
If shoulders hurt, add face pulls.
For novices, one ab isolation exercise plus compound movements is enough; planks, leg raises or crunches all work.
Novices training 3 days a week at this workload don't need GPP on off days.
Running a 3-day novice program twice a week works but yields less gains.
Adding calf and neck work at the end of the program is fine.
Novices should get a taste of isolation work including direct forearm work (e.g. hammer curls), even though pull-ups and pulls train forearms.
Anything works for novices, and this program is written effectively, so it will work.
